newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Peters unrattled by gloomy forecast for NZ.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Peters unrattled by gloomy forecast for NZ.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters said on Wednesday he stood by Treasury's rosy economic forecasts despite a much darker picture painted by investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG).

Peters and Treasury Secretary Murray Horn, under grilling by Parliament's powerful Finance and Expenditure select committee, were unmoved by private sector views they are too optimistic and fail to account for a slowdown recorded since the June budget.
Peters said growth would average 3.4 percent over the next three years, as the rate of Gross Domestic Product growth rises from 2.4 percent this financial year to 4.2 percent next year.
"This is a realistic forecast, and not wildly optimistic as some have suggested," he told the parliamentarians.
He said economic data suggesting a slowdown published since the budget had not caused him to alter his view.

But DMG Chief Economist Ulf Schoefisch, the central Reserve Bank's former head of forecasting, on Wednesday published a report saying growth this year would be just 1.2 percent and would only rise to 2.5 and 2.7 percent in succeeding years.
The consequences of the slower rates would be significant, including dashing chances for further tax cuts after 1998 and seeing the unemployment rate rise to 8.0 percent from 6.4.

If DMG's scenario proves correct, it could also have severe political ramification for Peters as he is battling to introduce a compulsory pension scheme that is linked to further rounds of tax cuts after a three percent reduction due next July.
A referendum on the scheme is due in September.
Asked to comment on the DMG report, Peters told reporters: "The whole mix of economic forecast analysis does not agree with that forecasting."
Schoefish said that even the low growth rates DMG is forecasting would only be achieved if there was a further significant easing in monetary policy in the near future.
He slated the Reserve Bank for being "overly cautious" and said monetary conditions were far above historical averages.
Schoefisch expected growing evidence of slow growth and falling inflation would convince the RB to ease more vigorously.

But Treasury's budget manager Mark Prebble told the parliamentary committee that even though GDP growth in the March quarter was negative 0.5 percent he saw no reason to change the department's forecasts.
"We still see that scenario," he told the committee, explaining that Treasury still believed growth rates would pick up in the second half of this year and into 1998.
He said it appeared most confidence surveys released recently had been gathered prior to the budget on June 26.
Peters said that since he became Treasurer in December, interest rates, inflation and the New Zealand dollar had all fallen sharply in line with the wishes of business.
He said real confidence could be measured by investment in the share market, which had undergone its sharpest surge since the "black" October of 1987.
He expressed frustration at the business community complaining about confidence falling, saying there was little more the government could do to improve the business environment.
"What more can we do? I admit there are things we must press harder on but it is time for them (the business community) to snap out of it," he said.
